Best Practices for Olink Protein Biomarker Discovery and Validation

OlinkViz Authors

2026-11-17

Source: vignettes/biomarker_discovery.Rmd
biomarker_discovery.Rmd

Abstract

Olink’s Proximity Extension Assay (PEA) has become a leading platform for high-throughput, high-sensitivity protein quantification in clinical cohort studies. Its core technology — pairs of oligonucleotide-labeled antibodies whose DNA strands hybridize and are extended upon proximal binding — enables multiplexed detection of 92 to over 5,400 proteins from minimal sample volumes (~1 µL of plasma), with readout by qPCR or NGS yielding Normalized Protein eXpression (NPX) values on a log₂ scale. This guide provides a practical, end-to-end roadmap for Olink-based biomarker discovery, covering study design, quality control, differential expression, machine learning, multi-protein signature construction, functional interpretation, and reporting standards. Every section is written specifically for the Olink practitioner, with code examples drawn from the OlinkViz package and its bundled datasets.

1. Introduction

1.1 The PEA Technology

The proximity extension assay (PEA) couples pairs of oligonucleotide-labeled antibodies that bind adjacent epitopes on a target protein. When both antibodies bind, their DNA strands hybridize and are extended by a DNA polymerase, creating a PCR-amplifiable amplicon unique to each protein. Quantification is performed by qPCR (Olink Target 96, Target 48) or NGS (Olink Explore), yielding NPX values — normalized log₂-transformed relative protein concentrations.

Key properties that shape the downstream analytical strategy:

  • NPX is on log₂ scale: Differences between groups are directly interpretable as log₂ fold changes. An NPX difference of +1 equals a 2-fold higher concentration; a difference of −0.58 equals approximately 0.67-fold (two-thirds).
  • One assay = one protein: Unlike discovery proteomics, there is no peptide identification, protein inference, or parsimony grouping step. Each Olink assay maps to a single, pre-validated protein target.
  • Missing values are predominantly MNAR (missing not at random): proteins fall below the assay’s limit of detection (LOD) because their true concentration is low. This has specific implications for imputation (see Section 3.5).
  • High sensitivity, wide dynamic range: ~10 logs from fM to µM, with intra-assay CVs of 5–15% and inter-assay CVs of 10–25%.
  • Panel-based coverage: Proteins are measured in pre-defined panels (Inflammation, Immune Response, Cardiometabolic, Neurology, Oncology, and the broader Explore panels). This is efficient but means pathway enrichment must account for the panel’s gene-set composition (see Section 7.1).

1.2 Olink Platforms at a Glance

Platform Readout Proteins Typical Use
Target 96 qPCR (Fluidigm BioMark) 92 per panel Focused hypothesis testing, targeted panels
Target 48 qPCR 44 per panel Custom mini-panels, signature validation
Explore 384 NGS (Illumina NovaSeq) ~368 Expanded discovery
Explore 1536 NGS ~1,472 Broad discovery
Explore 3072 NGS ~2,944 Comprehensive plasma proteome
Explore HT NGS ~5,400 Largest PEA panel; proteome-wide

1.3 What This Guide Covers

  • Study design: Sample sizes, power, the three-phase biomarker framework
  • Data preprocessing: QC, normalization, replicate handling, missing value imputation
  • Differential expression: Test selection, multiple testing strategy, confounder adjustment
  • Machine learning: Nested cross-validation, algorithm selection, feature stability
  • Signature building: Composite scores, ROC evaluation, reporting standards
  • Functional interpretation: Pathway enrichment with panel-aware backgrounds
  • Reproducibility: Reporting standards and project structure

2. Study Design

2.1 The Three-Phase Biomarker Development Framework

Protein biomarker development, regardless of measurement platform, follows a well-characterized three-phase pipeline. Each phase serves a distinct purpose and uses progressively stricter statistical thresholds:

┌─────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────┐
│  Phase 1: Discovery │ →  │ Phase 2: Verification │ →  │ Phase 3: Validation  │
│  n = 20-100/group   │    │  n = 100-500/group     │    │  n = 500-5,000+/group│
│  Broad panels       │    │  Focused panel/custom  │    │  Custom targeted     │
│  Liberal thresholds │    │  FDR < 0.05            │    │  Strict significance │
│  Goal: include      │    │  Independent cohort    │    │  Multi-site cohorts  │
└─────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────┘    └──────────────────────┘

Phase 1: Discovery

  • Sample size: 20–100 per group. Small N risks false negatives; large N without adequate power planning risks identifying statistically significant but biologically irrelevant differences. Use prospective power calculations (Section 2.2).
  • Panel selection: Choose the broadest panel(s) relevant to your disease biology. For inflammatory or autoimmune conditions, combine Olink Target 96 Inflammation + Immune Response (184 proteins). For broader discovery or hypothesis-free work, use Explore 1536, 3072, or HT.
  • Statistical approach: Use a liberal threshold — nominal p < 0.05 without correction, or a relaxed FDR of 10–20%. The goal is sensitivity: include as many true candidates as possible. Specificity will be handled in later phases.
  • Fold-change filter: Require a minimum effect size (e.g., |log₂FC| > 0.5, ~1.4-fold). This eliminates proteins with statistically detectable but biologically trivial differences.
  • Output: A ranked candidate list of 15–50 proteins.
# Phase 1 discovery with OlinkViz
library(OlinkViz)
library(dplyr)

data("bansal_baseline57")

# Per-protein Wilcoxon: Healthy vs Long COVID
long_data <- bansal_baseline57 %>%
  filter(`Long_COVID status` %in% c("Healthy", "Long COVID"))

discovery_results <- lapply(unique(long_data$Assay), function(prot) {
  sub <- long_data %>% filter(Assay == prot)
  test <- wilcox.test(
    NPX ~ `Long_COVID status`,
    data = sub,
    exact = FALSE
  )
  data.frame(
    Assay  = prot,
    p.value = test$p.value,
    mean_healthy = mean(sub$NPX[sub$`Long_COVID status` == "Healthy"], na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_lc      = mean(sub$NPX[sub$`Long_COVID status` == "Long COVID"], na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}) %>% bind_rows()

discovery_results$log2FC <- discovery_results$mean_lc - discovery_results$mean_healthy

# Phase 1 filters: nominal p < 0.05, |log2FC| > 0.5
candidates <- discovery_results %>%
  filter(p.value < 0.05, abs(log2FC) > 0.5) %>%
  arrange(p.value)

plot_volcano(discovery_results, title = "Phase 1: Discovery")

Phase 2: Verification

  • Sample size: 100–500 per group, drawn from an independent cohort. This is the single most important step for eliminating false discoveries.
  • Approach: Test only the candidate proteins from Phase 1. If using Olink Target 96, you may design a custom panel or measure candidates via individual assays. For Explore datasets, subset the analysis to the candidate list.
  • Statistical threshold: Apply Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction at FDR < 0.05. All candidates passing this threshold advance to Phase 3.
  • Output: A refined list of 5–15 proteins.
# Phase 2 runs on an independent dataset
candidates_verified <- candidates %>%
  mutate(p_adj = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")) %>%
  filter(p_adj < 0.05)

Phase 3: Clinical Validation

  • Sample size: 500–5,000+, ideally multi-site with broad demographic representation.
  • Approach: Pre-specify the full analysis — the protein signature from Phase 2, the statistical model, thresholds, and clinical endpoint. Register the analysis plan (ClinicalTrials.gov or OSF) before execution.
  • Output: A validated biomarker signature with sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV estimated in the target population.

2.2 Sample Size and Power

Power calculations for Olink studies must account for:

  • Multiple testing burden: For a Target 96 panel (92 proteins), Bonferroni correction requires α = 0.05/92 ≈ 5.4 × 10⁻⁴ per protein. In practice, use BH-FDR at 5% for verification/validation phases.
  • Realistic effect sizes: Clinically meaningful plasma protein differences are often modest — 1.2–1.8 fold (log₂FC = 0.26–0.85). Power calculations should use effect sizes drawn from prior literature, not optimistic guesses.
  • Olink CVs: Intra-assay CV 5–15%, inter-assay CV 10–25%. Use the upper bound for conservative planning.

Practical sample-size guidelines for Olink Target 96 discovery (80% power, α = 0.05, two-sided two-sample t-test):

Target fold change log₂FC N per group
1.2-fold ~0.26 ~90
1.5-fold ~0.58 ~25
2.0-fold ~1.0 ~10

For FDR-controlled analysis across 92 proteins, multiply per-group N by ~1.5–2×. For Explore 3072, use BH-FDR throughout and increase sample sizes proportionally.

3. Data Preprocessing and Quality Control

3.1 Olink Data Structure

Olink delivers data in a standardized long format. The key columns are:

Column Description Common Names
SampleID Unique sample identifier SampleID, SubjectID, Participant
Assay Protein/gene name Assay, Protein, Target
NPX Normalized log₂ protein expression NPX, Value
Panel Olink panel name Panel
LOD Limit of detection LOD
QC Warning Quality flag QC Warning, Warning

OlinkViz detects these columns automatically via detect_columns() and validates the data structure with validate_npx().

3.2 Quality Control

3.2.1 Visual QC First — Before Any Statistical Test

The first step in every Olink analysis is a visual survey of the data. Batch effects, whether from plates, reagent lots, or run order, are the #1 cause of false discoveries.

# PCA colored by potential sources of unwanted variation
plot_dim_reduc(my_data, type = "pca", color = "Plate")
plot_dim_reduc(my_data, type = "pca", color = "Panel")
plot_dim_reduc(my_data, type = "pca", color = "Group")

# Heatmap of top variable proteins — reveals outlier samples at a glance
plot_heatmap(my_data, scale = "row", show_rownames = FALSE)

# Sample correlation — detects swaps and gross outliers
plot_corr(my_data, method = "spearman", top_n = 50)

3.2.2 Sample-Level QC 

sample_qc <- my_data %>%
  group_by(SampleID) %>%
  summarise(
    n_detected   = sum(!is.na(NPX)),
    n_total      = n(),
    frac_missing = mean(is.na(NPX)),
    mean_npx     = mean(NPX, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_npx       = sd(NPX, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Flag samples with >30% missing or mean NPX > 3 SD from grand mean
grand_mean <- mean(sample_qc$mean_npx, na.rm = TRUE)
grand_sd   <- sd(sample_qc$mean_npx, na.rm = TRUE)
flagged <- sample_qc %>%
  filter(frac_missing > 0.30 | abs(mean_npx - grand_mean) > 3 * grand_sd)

3.2.3 Protein-Level QC

Proteins with a high proportion of values below LOD need careful handling:

Fraction below LOD Action
>50% Consider exclusion (insufficient dynamic range); retain only if biologically essential
20–50% Retain, with left-censored imputation (Section 3.5)
<20% Retain with standard handling 
protein_qc <- my_data %>%
  group_by(Assay) %>%
  summarise(
    n_below_lod    = sum(NPX < LOD, na.rm = TRUE),
    frac_below_lod = mean(NPX < LOD, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_npx       = mean(NPX, na.rm = TRUE),
    cv             = sd(NPX, na.rm = TRUE) / abs(mean(NPX, na.rm = TRUE)),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

3.3 Normalization

Olink NPX values are already normalized during the NPX Manager pipeline (extension control normalization, inter-plate adjustment, and log₂ transformation). Do not apply additional normalization unless a specific batch effect is visually confirmed.

When batch effects are present despite Olink’s internal normalization (e.g., different reagent lots, plate effects identifiable on PCA), consider:

  1. Including batch as a model covariate — the preferred approach. Add + Plate or + Batch to your statistical model rather than pre-correcting the data. This preserves biological signal while adjusting for technical variation.
  2. ComBat (sva::ComBat()) — parametric batch correction for when the model-inclusion approach isn’t feasible. Requires adequate sample size per batch.
  3. limma::removeBatchEffect() — use only for visualization, not as input to downstream statistical tests.

Always compare PCA plots before and after any batch correction. A correction that collapses genuine biological separation alongside batch effects has done more harm than good.

3.4 Replicate Measurements

  • Intra-assay replicates (same plate): Average NPX values. Report the CV.
  • Inter-assay replicates (different plates/runs): Average after confirming acceptable CV (<25%), or use a mixed-effects model with plate as a random effect.

OlinkViz’s to_wide() averages replicates automatically:

wide <- to_wide(my_data)
# Auto-detected columns: sample_col = 'SampleID'
# Averaged 8 replicate(s) across 2 plate(s)

3.5 Missing Value Imputation

Missing values in Olink data are predominantly MNAR (missing not at random): the protein concentration is below the assay’s LOD. This is fundamentally different from stochastic missingness and requires a different imputation approach.

Imputation Methods (Ordered by Preference for Olink Data)

  1. Down-shift imputation (recommended): Draw from a Gaussian centered at (LOD − 1.8σ) with σ = 0.3 × SD(observed values). This preserves the left-censored structure of the data.
  2. Minimal value replacement: Replace with LOD or LOD/√2. Simple, conservative, widely used in the Olink literature.
  3. Quantile regression imputation (imputeLCMD): More sophisticated, dataset-adaptive left-censored imputation.
  4. KNN imputation: Only for technical (MCAR) missingness — e.g., a sample with a processing error. Do not use for values below LOD.

Never use mean imputation. It systematically overestimates low-abundance proteins — the proteins most likely to differ between disease states — and attenuates fold changes exactly where they matter most.

impute_left_censored <- function(npx_values, lod_values) {
  below <- which(npx_values < lod_values)
  if (length(below) == 0) return(npx_values)

  observed <- npx_values[npx_values >= lod_values]
  sd_obs <- sd(observed, na.rm = TRUE)

  set.seed(42)
  imputed_values <- rnorm(
    length(below),
    mean = lod_values[below] - 1.8 * sd_obs,
    sd   = 0.3 * sd_obs
  )
  npx_values[below] <- imputed_values
  npx_values
}

4. Statistical Analysis

4.1 Choosing the Right Test

Scenario Recommended Method Notes
Two-group, n < 20/group Wilcoxon rank-sum Robust to non-normality; exact = FALSE
Two-group, n ≥ 20/group Moderated t-test (limma) Gold standard — borrows strength across proteins
Paired / longitudinal Linear mixed model (lmer) Random intercept per subject; handles missing visits
Multi-group Kruskal-Wallis or one-way ANOVA Follow with pairwise post-hoc tests
Continuous outcome Spearman correlation or linear regression NPX ~ clinical_variable
Adjusted analysis limma or ANCOVA with covariates ~ group + age + sex + bmi

Moderated t-tests via limma are the gold standard for Olink differential expression. By borrowing variance information across all proteins on the panel, limma produces stable variance estimates even when n per group is small — a common scenario in Olink studies where n = 10–30 per group is typical.

library(limma)

# Prepare wide matrix: rows = proteins, columns = samples
wide_matrix <- to_wide(my_data) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames("Assay") %>%
  as.matrix()

# Design matrix
group <- factor(col_data$Group)
design <- model.matrix(~ group)

# Fit and moderate
fit <- lmFit(wide_matrix, design)
fit <- eBayes(fit)

# Extract results
results <- topTable(fit, coef = 2, number = Inf, adjust.method = "BH")

# Visualize
plot_volcano(results, pval_col = "adj.P.Val", fc_col = "logFC",
             title = "limma: Differential Expression")

4.2 Multiple Testing Strategy by Phase

The appropriate correction depends on the study phase — do not apply the same threshold everywhere:

Phase Correction Rationale
Discovery Nominal p < 0.05, or relaxed FDR 10–20% Maximize sensitivity; false positives are filtered in verification
Verification BH-FDR < 0.05 Balance; independent cohort adds protection
Validation BH-FDR < 0.05 or Bonferroni Pre-specified analysis; strict control required
Exploratory Report nominal and adjusted Full transparency

Common pitfall: Applying Bonferroni correction to a Phase 1 discovery study with 184 proteins (two Target 96 panels). This eliminates most true positives while only marginally improving specificity — directly defeating the purpose of a discovery phase.

4.3 Interpreting Fold Changes in NPX Space

Because NPX is on log₂ scale, the difference between two group means is the log₂ fold change:

  • mean_NPX_case − mean_NPX_control = +1.0 → 2× higher in cases
  • mean_NPX_case − mean_NPX_control = +0.58 → 1.5× higher
  • mean_NPX_case − mean_NPX_control = −1.0 → 0.5× (half) in cases
  • mean_NPX_case − mean_NPX_control = −0.58 → ~0.67× (two-thirds) in cases

Use both statistical significance and biological significance (fold change) for candidate prioritization:

  • |log₂FC| > 0.5 (~1.4-fold): Minimum meaningful change for most plasma proteins.
  • |log₂FC| > 1.0 (2-fold): Strong effect — prioritize for verification.
  • Detected in one group, below LOD in the other: Biologically meaningful even if the numerical NPX difference is small — flag separately; do not let the small numerical delta bury this signal.

4.4 Confounders and Covariate Adjustment

Plasma protein levels are influenced by more than disease status. Common confounders in Olink studies:

Category Variables
Demographic Age, sex, BMI
Pre-analytical Fasting status, time of day, anticoagulant (EDTA vs. citrate vs. heparin), storage duration, freeze-thaw cycles
Clinical Comorbidities, medications, disease severity
Technical Plate, plate position, run order, reagent lot

Workflow: 1. Record all potential confounders at sample collection. 2. Check for imbalance between groups (t-test, chi-squared). 3. Adjust for imbalanced covariates in the model: ~ group + age + sex + bmi + Plate. 4. Report unadjusted and adjusted results; concordance strengthens confidence.

5. Machine Learning for Biomarker Discovery

5.1 Nested Cross-Validation

The most consequential statistical error in biomarker discovery is reporting model performance evaluated on the same data used for feature selection and training. This produces catastrophically overfitted AUC estimates — an AUC of 0.95 from a study that selected features and evaluated the model on the same N = 30 samples is not impressive; it is expected under random chance alone.

The solution is nested (double) cross-validation:

Outer CV loop (5-fold): estimate generalization performance
  ├─ Inner CV loop (3-5 fold): select features and tune hyperparameters
  │   ├─ Feature selection (e.g., top-k by t-test, or L1 regularization)
  │   ├─ Model training with selected features
  │   └─ Hyperparameter tuning
  └─ Evaluate on held-out outer fold
→ Report mean ± SD of outer-fold AUC
library(caret)

ctrl <- trainControl(
  method = "repeatedcv",
  number = 5,
  repeats = 5,
  search = "grid"
)

set.seed(123)
lasso_fit <- train(
  x = wide_matrix,
  y = factor(group_labels),
  method = "glmnet",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneLength = 20
)

Red flag: Any study reporting a biomarker panel discovered and evaluated on the same samples without nested CV or an independent validation cohort is presenting performance estimates that are systematically and often dramatically inflated.

5.2 Algorithm Selection for Olink

Algorithm Strengths When to Use
Lasso (L1) Built-in feature selection; interpretable coefficients Typical Olink: p = 92–184, n = 50–200
Elastic Net Handles correlated predictors well When proteins co-vary strongly (common in Olink panels)
Random Forest Captures non-linear relationships; robust to outliers Larger n; pair with permutation importance
SVM (RBF) Effective with small n and complex boundaries Two-group classification with n < 50/group
Penalized logistic regression Well-calibrated probabilities; interpretable ORs Case-control designs where interpretability matters

5.3 Panel-Aware Feature Selection

Olink panels contain groups of functionally related proteins (e.g., multiple chemokines in the Inflammation panel). Two practical considerations:

  • Correlation-aware selection: Lasso selects one representative from each correlated group. Elastic net retains the group. Choose based on whether you want a minimal signature (Lasso) or a redundant, robust one (Elastic Net).
  • Stability analysis: Run feature selection on 100 bootstrap resamples; report how often each protein is selected. Proteins selected in >50% of resamples are stable candidates.
  • Panel dominance check: If using multiple panels (e.g., Inflammation + Immune Response), verify the final signature isn’t dominated by one panel — this may indicate a panel-level batch artifact.

6. Multi-Protein Signatures

6.1 Building a Composite Score

Individual proteins rarely provide sufficient discriminatory power for clinical use. A multi-protein composite score almost always outperforms any single marker.

Approach 1: Sign-Weighted Z-Score Sum

For each protein, compute a z-score within the cohort, multiply by +1 (higher in disease) or −1 (lower in disease), then sum across the signature. This approach is simple, requires no model training, and is used in the OlinkViz paper-inspired workflows:

# Step 1: Determine direction from univariate AUC
prot_direction <- bansal_baseline57 %>%
  filter(`Long_COVID status` %in% c("Healthy", "Long COVID")) %>%
  group_by(Assay) %>%
  summarise(
    auc = as.numeric(pROC::auc(
      pROC::roc(as.integer(`Long_COVID status` == "Long COVID"), NPX, quiet = TRUE)
    )),
    direction = ifelse(auc >= 0.5, 1, -1),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Step 2: Compute z-scores and aggregate
signature_proteins <- c("CXCL10", "IL6", "CCL2", "TNF", "IFNG")
signature_scores <- bansal_baseline57 %>%
  filter(Assay %in% signature_proteins) %>%
  left_join(prot_direction, by = "Assay") %>%
  group_by(Assay) %>%
  mutate(z_npx = as.numeric(scale(NPX))) %>%
  group_by(SampleID, `Long_COVID status`) %>%
  summarise(
    signature_score = sum(direction * z_npx, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

Approach 2: Model-Weighted Score

Use coefficients from a fitted model (lasso, elastic net, or logistic regression) as weights:

sig_data <- wide_matrix[, signature_proteins]
fit <- glm(group_labels ~ ., data = as.data.frame(sig_data), family = binomial)
composite_score <- predict(fit, newdata = as.data.frame(sig_data), type = "link")

Approach 3: PCA-Based Score

Use PC1 of the signature proteins as the composite score. This captures the dominant co-variation pattern without requiring outcome labels, but loses directionality — the sign of PC1 is arbitrary.

6.2 Evaluating Signature Performance

For individual proteins or pre-computed signature scores, plot_roc() draws empirical or binormal-smoothed ROC curves with DeLong 95% CIs and optional bootstrap sensitivity ribbons (add_ci = TRUE, smooth_method = "binormal"):

library(pROC)

# Multi-protein smoothed ROC curves with 95% bootstrap sensitivity ribbons
plot_roc(
  bansal_baseline57[bansal_baseline57$`Long_COVID status` %in% c("Healthy", "Long COVID"), ],
  assays        = c("CXCL10", "IL6", "CCL2", "TNF"),
  group         = "Long_COVID status",
  smooth_method = "binormal",
  add_ci        = TRUE,
  show_direction = TRUE
)

roc_obj <- pROC::roc(
  signature_scores$`Long_COVID status` == "Long COVID",
  signature_scores$signature_score
)
plot(roc_obj, main = "Signature ROC", print.auc = TRUE, print.auc.cex = 1.2)

Minimum reporting standards for a biomarker signature: - AUC with 95% CI (DeLong method) - Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV at the Youden-optimal threshold - The same metrics at one or more pre-specified, clinically motivated thresholds - Explicit statement if the threshold was optimized on the evaluation data - For Phase 3: pre-registration of the analysis plan

7. Functional Interpretation

7.1 Pathway Enrichment — Panel-Aware Background

OlinkViz provides enrich_pathways(), a wrapper around gProfiler2 supporting GO, KEGG, Reactome, and WikiPathways:

de_proteins <- discovery_results %>%
  filter(p.value < 0.05) %>%
  pull(Assay)

enrichment <- enrich_pathways(
  de_proteins,
  sources = c("GO:BP", "KEGG", "REAC"),
  p_cutoff = 0.05
)

Critical: Olink panels are not random samples of the proteome. Each panel is designed around a biological theme — the Inflammation panel is enriched for chemokines, cytokines, and acute phase proteins. If you test inflammatory-disease DE proteins against the whole-genome background, every immune-related pathway will appear highly significant because your input list is pre-enriched for it.

Solution: Supply the full Olink panel gene list as the custom background (custom_bg argument in gost()). This asks: “Among the proteins we actually measured, which pathways are over-represented in the DE set?” rather than the misleading “Among all ~20,000 human genes, which pathway terms appear?”.

7.2 Protein-Protein Interaction Networks 

# STRING PPI network
plot_network(de_proteins[1:30], required_score = 500)

# Correlation-based network
plot_corr(my_data, top_n = 25, display_method = "color")

7.3 Clinical Variable Correlations

Linking Olink protein levels to clinical measurements — vital signs, lab values, disease severity scores — establishes face validity and suggests functional relevance. See scripts/generate_figures_jir.R for a complete worked example from the Tan et al. (2025) AMI biomarker template.

8. Reproducibility and Reporting Standards

8.1 Minimum Reporting Checklist

  1. Pre-analytical
    • Sample type, collection tube, anticoagulant
    • Centrifugation, time to freezer, storage temperature and duration
    • Freeze-thaw cycles, fasting status
  2. Olink assay
    • Panel name(s), version, lot number
    • Platform and readout method
    • Number of plates, plate layout, randomization scheme
    • Internal control performance (Incubation, Detection, Extension controls)
  3. Data processing
    • Software version (NPX Manager or Olink Analyze)
    • QC exclusion criteria for samples and assays
    • Missing value handling: proportion below LOD per assay, imputation method
    • Batch correction method (if any)
  4. Statistical analysis
    • Statistical test and rationale
    • Multiple testing correction
    • Covariates in adjusted models
    • Software: R version, package versions (sessionInfo())
  5. Biomarker evaluation (Phase 2–3)
    • Pre-specified analysis plan (registration recommended)
    • Sample size justification
    • Model features, training procedure, threshold selection
    • Validation strategy: CV scheme (internal), independent cohort (external)
    • Performance metrics with confidence intervals

8.2 Reproducible Project Structure 

my_olink_study/
├── data/
│   ├── raw/           # Untouched Olink NPX Manager exports
│   └── processed/     # QC'd, imputed, normalized data
├── scripts/
│   ├── 01_qc.R
│   ├── 02_preprocess.R
│   ├── 03_differential_expression.R
│   ├── 04_biomarker_modeling.R
│   └── 05_figures.R
├── output/
│   ├── figures/
│   └── tables/
├── renv.lock          # Package version control
└── my_olink_study.Rproj

End every analysis with sessionInfo().

9. Common Pitfalls

Pitfall Consequence Solution
Using t-test with n = 3/group No variance estimation; p-values meaningless Moderated t-test (limma) or Wilcoxon for n < 10
No covariate adjustment Spurious associations from age/sex/BMI confounding Record and adjust for known confounders
Overfitting in small samples “AUC = 0.99” that vanishes on replication Nested CV; external validation cohort
Whole-genome background for enrichment Inflated significance for panel-relevant pathways Use Olink panel gene list as enrichment background
Mean imputation for below-LOD values Attenuated fold changes; false negatives Left-censored imputation (Section 3.5)
Discovery and validation on same samples Grossly overestimated performance Physically separate cohorts, or nested CV at minimum
Bonferroni in Phase 1 discovery Eliminated true candidates Relaxed thresholds in discovery; correct in verification
Treating NPX as linear concentration Misinterpreted fold changes NPX is log₂: differences ARE log₂ fold changes
Comparing NPX across panel versions without bridging Apparent differences are platform artifacts Bridging study with overlapping samples

10. Practical Workflow 

library(OlinkViz)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(pROC)

# 1. Load and inspect
data("bansal_baseline57")
validate_npx(bansal_baseline57)

# 2. QC
plot_dim_reduc(bansal_baseline57, type = "pca", color = "Panel", ellipse = TRUE)
plot_heatmap(bansal_baseline57, scale = "row", show_rownames = FALSE)

# 3. Differential expression
long_data <- bansal_baseline57 %>%
  filter(`Long_COVID status` %in% c("Healthy", "Long COVID"))

de_results <- long_data %>%
  group_by(Assay) %>%
  summarise(
    p.value = wilcox.test(NPX ~ `Long_COVID status`, exact = FALSE)$p.value,
    mean_hc = mean(NPX[`Long_COVID status` == "Healthy"], na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_lc = mean(NPX[`Long_COVID status` == "Long COVID"], na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    log2FC = mean_lc - mean_hc,
    p_adj  = p.adjust(p.value, method = "BH")
  )

# 4. Volcano plot
plot_volcano(de_results, pval_threshold = 0.05, fc_threshold = 0.5,
             title = "Healthy vs Long COVID")

# 5. Top candidates
top_hits <- de_results %>%
  filter(p_adj < 0.05) %>%
  slice_min(p.value, n = 6)

plot_boxplot(long_data, assay = top_hits$Assay[1], group = "Long_COVID status")
plot_corr(long_data %>% filter(Assay %in% top_hits$Assay),
          method = "spearman", top_n = 20)

# 6. Pathway enrichment
enrich_pathways(
  de_results %>% filter(p.value < 0.05) %>% pull(Assay),
  sources = c("GO:BP", "KEGG")
)

# 7. Signature construction → see scripts/generate_figures_paper.R

11. Further Reading

  1. Al-Nesf et al. (2022). Prognostic tools and candidate drugs based on plasma proteomics of patients with severe COVID-19 complications. Nature Communications, 13:2406. — Olink-based 12-protein severity signature with ROC, clustering, and network analysis across 893 proteins and three Olink panels.

  2. Tan et al. (2025). Identification of Cardiometabolic Protein Biomarkers for Acute Myocardial Infarction Using Olink Proteomics. Journal of Inflammation Research. — Olink Target 96 Cardiometabolic panel for AMI biomarker discovery with GO/KEGG enrichment, STRING PPI, and combined ROC.

  3. Assarsson et al. (2014). Homogenous 96-Plex PEA Immunoassay Exhibiting High Sensitivity, Specificity, and Excellent Scalability. PLOS ONE, 9(4):e95192. — Foundational PEA technology paper; assay performance characteristics, dynamic range, cross-reactivity data.

  4. Rifai et al. (2006). Protein biomarker discovery and validation: the long and uncertain path to clinical utility. Nature Biotechnology, 24(8):971–983. — The canonical three-phase biomarker development framework.

  5. Broadhurst & Kell (2006). Statistical strategies for avoiding false discoveries in metabolomics and related experiments. Metabolomics, 2(4):171–196. — Essential reading on multiple testing, cross-validation pitfalls, and overfitting in omics biomarker studies.

  6. Lazar et al. (2016). Accounting for the Multiple Natures of Missing Values in Label-Free Quantitative Proteomics Data Sets to Compare Imputation Strategies. Journal of Proteome Research, 15(4):1116–1125. — Framework for choosing imputation methods based on missingness mechanism.

  7. Olink (2023). Data normalization and standardization. Olink Proteomics Technical Note. — NPX normalization pipeline, QC metrics, and data interpretation guidelines.

  8. OlinkViz vignettes: vignette("OlinkViz") for the visualization cookbook; scripts/generate_figures_paper.R and scripts/generate_figures_jir.R for end-to-end biomarker analysis workflows using the bundled datasets.
